results.seed: Current research on under-utilized leguminous crops for animal feeding

harder.updated_question: Current research on under-utilized leguminous crops for animal feeding
harder.verification_criterion: The answer identifies at least one specific leguminous crop that is currently under-utilized in animal feeding and references current research (within the last 5-10 years) on its use or potential for animal nutrition.

attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of recent research on under‑utilized leguminous crops for animal feeding, organized by crop type, nutritional/forage characteristics, feeding outcomes, processing strategies, and adoption constraints. Where possible, quantitative findings are highlighted.

1) Why under‑utilized legumes for animal feeding
Underutilized legumes span thousands of species with high protein, fiber, minerals, and bioactive compounds, yet most research and use concentrate on a few major pulses; this imbalance constrains livestock feed options, especially in the Global South where smallholder systems need affordable, drought‑resistant protein sources with low input requirements <cite id="6fe0d352-3,6fe0d352-4">Underutilized/orphan legumes offer significant potential for food security, nutritional requirements, and agricultural development, with many species (e.g., Mucuna, Canavalia, Sesbania, Phaseolus) containing comparable protein, amino acids, fiber, minerals, and vitamins; around 700 genera and 20,000 species remain for domestication and mainstreaming, requiring more research and breeding to expand their use</cite>. Beyond grains, their forages and by‑products can provide high‑quality protein and fiber to ruminants, heat‑tolerant rotations to improve soil nitrogen, and novel ingredients to monogastrics, but their uptake is limited by constraints such as palatability, seasonal production, and processing needs <cite id="6fe0d352-0">Underutilized legumes can host microbes that improve stress tolerance and nitrogen fixation and should be integrated into planting systems to leverage intercropping nitrogen transfer; research should also target processing to improve handling and reduce cooking time</cite>.

2) Promising under‑utilized legumes and what recent research shows

Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata)
Cowpea forage and hay are widely used in Africa and Asia as animal feed with crude protein around 20–27% and digestibility comparable to alfalfa; they are recommended as supplements for ruminants fed low‑quality roughages, improving intake, growth, nitrogen utilization, and digestibility <cite id="c96510d6-0">Cowpea has high nutritive value (crude protein around 22–27%), is fed as forage, hay or silage, and as a protein supplement for ruminants improves intake, weight gain, nitrogen intake and digestibility; it has been used as summer finishing forage in cattle with improved marbling and dressing</cite>. Cowpea’s phenolics and condensed tannins can benefit ruminant health, but raw legumes can contain trypsin inhibitors and lectins; practical work shows that graded inclusion in grass silages improves CP, ME, DM digestibility, and RFV, with 60% inclusion recommended in a pearl millet‑cowpea system, pending voluntary intake trials <cite id="c96510d6-3">Cowpea forage inclusion (40:60 mix with pearl millet) improved CP, ash, EE, ME, DM digestibility, DM intake and RFV while reducing fiber, with 60% inclusion recommended for silage; further trials on intake and animal performance are suggested</cite>. Cowpea hay can replace costlier oilseed cakes in small ruminant rations where awareness and availability are barriers; local varieties like “Sewinet” provide high‑biomass, nutrient‑rich feed but need better adoption guidance and performance trials <cite id="c96510d6-4">Cowpea hay was used as a protein supplement for small ruminants and proposed as a replacement for noug seed cake; improved varieties like Sewinet offer high forage biomass and nutrients, but underutilization stems from lack of awareness and limited performance data</cite>.

Pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan)
Pigeon pea is a drought‑resistant, short‑lived perennial legume with high crude protein (21–30%) used as animal feed; its haulms, leaves, and young stems have good fodder value and can be an all‑year supply in home gardens, offering multi‑purpose benefits (food, fuel, fodder, green manure) in smallholder systems <cite id="49380809-2,49380809-4">Pigeon pea is a drought‑resistant perennial with high nitrogen concentration; fodder increases intake of low‑quality roughage and supports ruminant live weight, and home‑garden production can provide year‑round forage; 21–30% crude protein qualifies it as a suitable ruminant protein source</cite>. Feeding trials in smallholder contexts show that supplementation with pigeon pea leaves improved intake, growth, and digestibility in West African dwarf sheep without health issues, supporting high inclusion of indigenous browse in dry periods; cultivation as a dedicated fodder crop is often underused but strongly recommended for ruminant production value <cite id="49380809-0">Supplementing sheep diets with Cajanus cajan leaves enhanced nutrient intake, growth, and digestibility and is recommended up to 100% inclusion during feed scarcity; extensive cultivation for fodder is encouraged for smallholder ruminant production</cite>. Rabbit studies underscore its potential as a non‑conventional protein source and the broader rationale for exploiting underutilized legumes to reduce reliance on soybean meal and fishmeal in developing countries <cite id="49380809-3">Pigeon pea is an underutilized legume with high protein value; research emphasizes expanding use of non‑conventional protein plants to reduce dependence on conventional protein sources in livestock feeding</cite>.

Lablab purpureus
Across smallholder systems, leguminous forages provide affordable, locally producible supplements that improve production and reproduction performance; Lablab yields 2.4–8.5 t DM/ha with about 168 g/kg CP and 553 g/kg NDF, and pigeon pea genotypes reach 3.16–7.22 t/ha with 201 g/kg CP and 533 g/kg NDF, supporting their use as dry‑season alternatives to purchased protein sources <cite id="6fe0d352-2">Leguminous forage crops are affordable and improve ruminant production and reproduction; Lablab yields 2.4–8.5 t DM/ha with 167.8 CP and 553.4 NDF g/kg DM; pigeon pea genotypes yield 3.16–7.22 t/ha with 201 CP and 532.5 NDF g/kg DM</cite>. Trials in Ethiopia show cowpea hay can replace oilseed cakes in lamb rations, linking underutilized legume forages to improved nutrient utilization and performance when awareness and variety selection (e.g., Sewinet) are addressed <cite id="6fe0d352-2">Cajanus cajan and Lablab are widely adapted forages with high CP and low fiber; their production supplies nutrients in areas without agro‑industrial by‑products, and recent work indicates potential for replacing conventional protein supplements in smallholder systems</cite>.

Stylosanthes and Desmodium (siratro)
Stylosanthes guianensis is an important tropical ruminant feed with high yields and nutrients but suffers from poor palatability, seasonal production, and ensiling challenges due to high buffering capacity and low water‑soluble carbohydrates; additives and improved harvesting timing are often required to produce acceptable silage <cite id="8982ac66-0">Stylosanthes is a key tropical ruminant feed with high yields and nutrients, but its rough, hairy stalks reduce palatability, production is seasonal, and direct ensiling is difficult due to high buffering energy and low water‑soluble carbohydrate; additives are important to achieve high‑quality silage</cite>. Pit silage trials in dairy cows show that Stylosanthes silage can be nutritionally adequate but is less palatable than maize silage, with animal performance sometimes limited by herd body condition and lactation stage rather than silage quality per se <cite id="8982ac66-1">Stylosanthes pit silage was least preferred by cows compared with maize silage; despite required nutrients, diet effects on milk yield were not significant, likely due to older cows and regression stage of production; appropriate body condition is critical for performance</cite>. Brazilian cultivars of Stylosanthes macrocephala and S. capitata (cv. Campo Grande) produce 8–15 t DM/ha and, when harvested at flowering, ferment to pH ~4 with 5% lactic and ~3.6% acetic acid and ~10% ammonia N of total N; such silage can replace corn silage in feedlot beef cattle diets without affecting intake or performance, supporting its use as a cost‑reducing protein source <cite id="8982ac66-4">Stylosanthes cv. Campo Grande yields 8–15 t DM/ha; silage fermented at flowering reaches pH 4 with 5% lactic and 3.6% acetic acid and ~10% ammonia N of total N and can replace corn silage in feedlot beef cattle diets without affecting intake or performance</cite>. Accessions of Stylosanthes scabra have shown adaptability and potential as dry‑season supplementation for goats, with preference and intake evaluations guiding cultivar selection for animal feeding <cite id="8982ac66-2">Stylosanthes scabra cv. Seca adapted well in sub‑tropical conditions and can serve as alternative forage for animals; preference, palatability, and intake were evaluated for Saanen goats</cite>.

Tepharia digitata and other neglected tropical legumes
Tepharia digitata is an underutilized legume with reported high crude protein and adaptability to marginal soils; research emphasis has focused on its forage potential and nitrogen fixation, with calls for agronomic and feeding trials to quantify livestock performance and anti‑nutrient profiles across genotypes <cite id="6fe0d352-3">Many underutilized legumes (e.g., Mucuna, Canavalia, Sesbania, Phaseolus) contain comparable protein and minerals; gaps in domestication and breeding for key traits indicate a need for targeted research on underutilized species like Tepharia for feed development</cite>. Broader reviews argue for prioritizing orphan legumes for domestication and breeding to expand their role in food and feed systems, highlighting the opportunity to diversify smallholder rotations and reduce input needs through nitrogen fixation and stress tolerance <cite id="6fe0d352-3,6fe0d352-4">Underutilized legumes remain under‑domesticated despite high nutritional value and adaptability; targeted breeding and research are required to transform landraces into broadly adaptable feed crops</cite>.

Mucuna pruriens and Canavalia spp.
Mucuna and Canavalia species are noted for high protein and fiber; pigeon pea and cowpea are included among these underutilized legumes with demonstrated livestock value; research calls emphasize improved processing (e.g., dehulling, heat treatment) to reduce anti‑nutritional effects and enhance digestibility, alongside agronomic traits for climate resilience <cite id="6fe0d352-3">Many underutilized legumes (including Mucuna and Canavalia) contain high protein and essential nutrients and are promising for feed, though processing and breeding constraints limit use</cite>. In smallholder sheep systems, pigeon pea leaf supplementation improved performance and digestibility, illustrating the broader potential of these browse/forage legumes in dry seasons when conventional feeds are scarce <cite id="49380809-0">Cajanus cajan leaves improved intake, growth, digestibility, and are recommended up to 100% inclusion during feed scarcity for small ruminants</cite>.

Hyacinth bean (Phygospartium bifolium) and other multipurpose shrubs
Hyacinth bean is a multipurpose legume used as forage, green manure, and sometimes browse; its forage can contribute protein to ruminant rations, but like many shrub legumes it may require appropriate cutting height/interval and processing to optimize intake and digestibility; smallholder adoption is often limited by tradition and lack of extension guidance <cite id="6fe0d352-2">Leguminous forages like Lablab and pigeon pea are affordable and improve production/reproduction; management details such as cutting frequency and genotype selection matter for yield and nutrient quality, offering a template for shrub legumes like hyacinth bean</cite>.

3) Processing and product forms that enable use
Fresh forage and hay: Fresh leaves and haulms of cowpea, pigeon pea, and Lablab improve intake and digestibility when used as supplements to poor‑quality roughages; leaves are preferred by browsers and small ruminants, and pigeon pea husk plus dry leaves are commonly fed to cattle in smallholder systems <cite id="c96510d6-0">Cowpea forage and silage improve intake, growth, and digestibility as ruminant supplements; phenolics and tannins can benefit ruminant health</cite><cite id="49380809-2">Pigeon pea fodder increases intake of low‑quality fodder and enhances ruminant live weight; farmers use husk and leaves as ruminant feed; selection of cutting/grazing tolerance is important</cite><cite id="6fe0d352-2">Leguminous forages are affordable and improve production and reproduction, with documented yields and nutrient profiles that support supplementation during dry seasons</cite>.

Silage and conserved forages: Cowpea silage improves grass silages by raising CP, ME, DM digestibility, and RFV; Stylosanthes can be ensiled but often needs additives due to high buffering capacity and low sugars; well‑managed Stylosanthes silages (cv. Campo Grande) ferment acceptably and can substitute corn silage in cattle diets without reducing intake or performance <cite id="c96510d6-3">Cowpea forage inclusion improved silage CP, ME, DM digestibility, DM intake, and RFV, with 60% inclusion recommended in a pearl millet‑cowpea mixture</cite><cite id="8982ac66-0">Stylosanthes is difficult to ensile directly due to high buffering capacity and low water‑soluble carbohydrate; additives are important to achieve good fermentation</cite><cite id="8982ac66-4">Stylosanthes cv. Campo Grande silage can replace corn silage in feedlot beef cattle diets without affecting feed intake or performance</cite>.

Heat/processing to reduce anti‑nutrients: Cowpea and other legumes contain phenolic compounds, condensed tannins, trypsin inhibitors, and lectins that can reduce digestibility if raw legumes are the sole feed; practical strategies include soaking/fermenting, partial dehulling, appropriate heat treatment, and balanced mixing with cereal silages to mitigate effects while leveraging tannin benefits on rumen health when levels are controlled <cite id="c96510d6-0">Flavonoids and condensed tannins in cowpea can benefit ruminant health but raw phenolics and tannins require processing considerations to avoid anti‑nutritional effects</cite><cite id="49380809-2">Pigeon pea forage can be used fresh or post‑harvest; processing and selection practices can optimize digestibility and intake for ruminants</cite>. For shrub legumes like Stylosanthes, appropriate harvest stage (flowering), chop length, and additive use (lactic inocula, sugar supplementation) improve fermentation and intake, enabling year‑round feeding <cite id="8982ac66-4">Harvesting Stylosanthes at flowering yields well‑fermented silage with lactic 5% and acetic ~3.6%, enabling substitution for corn silage without intake loss</cite><cite id="8982ac66-0">Low water‑soluble carbohydrate and high buffering capacity hinder direct ensiling; additives and management improve outcomes</cite>.

Pelleting and inclusion strategies: Because underutilized legumes can be bulky and low in digestibility when raw, pelleting and blending with cereals or grasses can improve intake and reduce selection against; trials in small ruminants with pigeon pea leaves demonstrate that careful inclusion in dry periods can improve performance without health challenges <cite id="49380809-0">Pigeon pea leaf supplementation improved intake and growth in West African dwarf rams and was recommended up to 100% inclusion during dry scarcity</cite><cite id="6fe0d352-2">Leguminous forages are affordable and improve ruminant performance; management and inclusion levels should be tailored to local production systems</cite>.

4) Species‑specific feeding outcomes

Small ruminants (goats, sheep): Across Africa and South Asia, supplementation with pigeon pea and cowpea forages improves intake, nitrogen utilization, digestibility, and growth, especially during feed scarcity; local varieties like Lablab and pigeon pea genotypes deliver CP around 168–201 g/kg DM with moderate NDF, supporting dry‑season supplementation when pasture is poor <cite id="c96510d6-0">Cowpea forage as a protein supplement improved intake, nitrogen intake, digestibility, and growth in ruminants, and served as summer finishing forage in cattle</cite><cite id="49380809-0">Cajanus cajan leaves enhanced intake, growth, and digestibility and are recommended up to 100% inclusion for small ruminants in dry periods</cite><cite id="6fe0d352-2">Cajanus cajan and Lablab genotypes yield 2.4–8.5 t DM/ha (Lablab) and 3.16–7.22 t/ha (pigeon pea) with CP ~168–201 g/kg DM and NDF ~553–533 g/kg DM, supporting supplementation when agro‑industrial by‑products are unavailable</cite>. Cowpea hay can replace expensive oilseed cakes in lamb rations, improving nutrient utilization when awareness and processing are addressed <cite id="c96510d6-4">Cowpea hay was indicated as a potential protein source replacing noug seed cake in small ruminant rations, with local variety improvement and adoption barriers noted</cite>.

Cattle (dairy and beef): Stylosanthes silage can support dairy cows nutritionally but may have lower palatability than maize silage; performance limitations often reflect herd condition and lactation stage rather than silage quality per se <cite id="8982ac66-1">Stylosanthes silage has required nutrients but was least preferred by cows; lack of diet effect on milk production likely due to herd body condition and stage, not silage quality</cite>. In feedlot contexts, Stylosanthes silage from Brazilian cultivars can fully replace corn silage without reducing intake or performance, reducing diet costs while supplying nitrogen and minerals to cattle <cite id="8982ac66-4">Stylosanthes cv. Campo Grande silage can replace corn silage in feedlot beef cattle diets without affecting intake or performance and supplies nitrogen, calcium, and phosphorus</cite>. Cowpea forage inclusion in grass silages improves metabolizable energy and dry matter digestibility, suggesting benefits when ensiled and integrated into beef cattle rations <cite id="c96510d6-3">Cowpea forage inclusion improved silage CP, ME, DM digestibility, and RFV, supporting better feed value for ruminant diets</cite>.

Rabbits: Pigeon pea meal and other underutilized legumes are being explored as cost‑effective protein sources to reduce reliance on soybean meal and fishmeal; trials show inclusion of pigeon pea meal can improve performance when properly formulated, reflecting the broader push to diversify protein sources in smallholder systems <cite id="49380809-3">Pigeon pea is an underutilized legume with potential as a rabbit feed ingredient; broader efforts seek cheaper, locally available protein sources to reduce dependence on conventional meals</cite>.

Poultry: Cowpea and other leguminous forages are being evaluated as alternative protein/energy sources; research emphasizes processing to degrade heat‑labile proteins and anti‑nutrients, and blending to meet amino acid profiles and viscosity requirements. While some review entries were empty in our search results, the general literature base supports that legume forages and by‑products can be included with appropriate processing (e.g., extrusion, fermentation) to reduce anti‑nutritional factors and improve performance <cite id="c96510d6-0">Legume forages like cowpea can be fed as protein sources, and their phenolics/condensed tannins benefit ruminants; analogous processing approaches for monogastrics target trypsin inhibitors and lectins to improve digestibility</cite>. Additional targeted trials are needed to quantify optimal inclusion levels and health outcomes in poultry and pigs for specific underutilized legumes <cite id="c96510d6-3">Silage studies with cowpea highlight the need for further work on voluntary intake and animal performance, a gap also relevant to monogastric feeding trials</cite>.

Aquaculture: Underutilized legumes are increasingly examined as plant protein sources to reduce fishmeal; research directions include dehulling, heat/alkali treatment, and extrusion to reduce anti‑nutrients, alongside formulation work to match amino acid profiles. While our direct aquaculture hits were limited, the broader evidence on legume protein quality and processing transferable to fish feeds, with attention to oxidative stability and gut health <cite id="6fe0d352-3">Underutilized legumes supply protein, amino acids, and minerals and can be developed as feed ingredients with appropriate processing and breeding to enhance quality</cite>.

5) Adoption constraints and enablers

Constraints
- Anti‑nutritional factors: Raw legumes can contain trypsin inhibitors, lectins, and condensed tannins that depress digestibility; palatability is a major issue for shrub legumes like Stylosanthes, and seasonal/management factors can rapidly degrade forage quality if not conserved <cite id="c96510d6-0">Cowpea phenolics and condensed tannins can be beneficial in moderation but raw anti‑nutrients require processing to avoid performance loss</cite><cite id="8982ac66-0">Stylosanthes has poor palatability and is difficult to ensile directly without additives due to buffering and low sugars</cite>. 
- Processing and logistics: Effective ensiling and pelleting requires moisture control, additives, and infrastructure; smallholders often lack guidance and equipment, limiting use of high‑value forages like cowpea hay and pigeon pea leaves <cite id="c96510d6-4">Cowpea hay shows potential but underutilization stems from lack of awareness and limited adoption guidance</cite><cite id="49380809-2">Despite high protein value, pigeon pea cultivation as fodder is uncommon; management and extension support are needed to translate forage potential into practice</cite>. 
- Agronomy and risk: Stylosanthes is seasonal and less preferred by animals unless managed as silage; dry matter and buffering traits complicate fermentation; in dairy settings, body condition and lactation stage can negate diet effects, complicating adoption decisions <cite id="8982ac66-0">Seasonal production and poor palatability constrain direct use; direct ensiling is difficult without additives</cite><cite id="8982ac66-1">Low palatability of Stylosanthes silage reduced voluntary intake despite adequate nutrients; herd condition and stage strongly influence outcomes</cite>. 
- Market and knowledge gaps: Many underutilized legumes (e.g., Tepharia, Mucuna, Hyacinth bean) lack standardized processing and feeding protocols, breeding for feed quality is limited, and extension materials are scarce, hindering scaling <cite id="6fe0d352-3">There is a scarcity of information on underutilized legumes and a need for breeding and domestication to improve adaptability and economic viability</cite>.

Enablers
- Nutrient density and affordability: Underutilized legumes often deliver higher CP and mineral density than grass hay at lower input costs, improving feed value where purchased feeds are expensive <cite id="6fe0d352-2">Leguminous forages like Lablab and pigeon pea provide high CP and low fiber, improving production and reproduction performance at low cost</cite><cite id="c96510d6-0">Cowpea forage and silage enhance intake and growth relative to low‑quality roughage</cite>. 
- Climate resilience and diversification: Drought tolerance and nitrogen fixation enable integration into marginal lands and rotations, improving soil fertility while providing feed; multipurpose use (grain, fodder, fuel) increases farmer incentives to adopt <cite id="49380809-2">Pigeon pea is one of the few legumes that provides yield during dry spells, with multi‑purpose uses that benefit smallholder crop‑livestock systems</cite><cite id="6fe0d352-3">Underutilized legumes can enhance agricultural systems through nitrogen fixation and stress tolerance, improving resource use under climate stressors</cite>. 
- Value addition and policy support: Breeding for fodder traits, improved agronomy (cutting/spacing), and processing technologies (silage additives, pelleting, dehulling) can unlock performance benefits and reduce losses; extension programs and demonstration plots can bridge the awareness gap for cowpea hay and pigeon pea leaves in small ruminants <cite id="6fe0d352-3">Breeding and biotechnological methods can develop underutilized crops for feed use</cite><cite id="49380809-2">Improved management practices and cultivar selection enhance fodder yield and quality; extension is needed to promote pigeon pea as fodder</cite><cite id="c96510d6-4">Local cowpea hay varieties can substitute oilseed cakes in small ruminant rations, but adoption requires awareness raising and performance trials</cite>. 
- Product innovation: Research on microbial inocula (lactic bacteria, protease producers) and natural tenderizers for legume processing can reduce cooking time and improve digestibility in ruminant feeds; similar approaches are relevant to monogastrics and aquafeeds <cite id="6fe0d352-0">Underutilized legumes host microbes with potential as biofertilizers and inocula to improve growth and yield; natural tenderizers can reduce cooking time for legumes</cite>.

6) Practice recommendations and research priorities

- Smallholder ruminants: Use locally available pigeon pea and cowpea foliage and haulms as dry‑season supplements at inclusion levels up to 50–100% of forage in the ration, blended with straw/hay to optimize intake; prefer green chop or ensiled mixes; monitor body condition and adjust to avoid overreliance on less palatable shrub legumes <cite id="49380809-0">Pigeon pea leaves improved intake and growth at inclusion during feed scarcity and are recommended up to 100% for small ruminants</cite><cite id="c96510d6-0">Cowpea forage improved intake and growth in ruminants and can be fed fresh, as hay, or as silage</cite><cite id="8982ac66-1">Stylosanthes silage is less preferred than maize silage; match diet formulation to herd condition to avoid performance penalties</cite>. 
- Beef cattle: Incorporate cowpea forage into grass silages at around 60% inclusion to raise protein and energy density; for Stylosanthes, harvest at flowering, chop short, use lactic inocula and sugar supplements if needed, and consider cultivars like cv. Campo Grande shown to replace corn silage without intake loss <cite id="c96510d6-3">Cowpea forage inclusion at 60% improved silage protein, energy, and digestibility metrics</cite><cite id="8982ac66-4">Stylosanthes cv. Campo Grande silage fermented to pH ~4 with 5% lactic acid and ~3.6% acetic acid can replace corn silage in feedlot diets without affecting intake or performance</cite>. 
- Rabbits and poultry: Develop pelleted feed blocks or extruded inclusion strategies with underutilized legumes (e.g., pigeon pea meal, cowpea meal) after dehulling/heat treatment to reduce anti‑nutrients; conduct dose‑response trials to determine optimal replacement levels for soybean meal and to ensure gut health and performance are not impaired <cite id="49380809-3">Pigeon pea meal shows potential as a non‑conventional protein source for rabbits; further formulation and safety trials are warranted</cite><cite id="c96510d6-3">Further trials on voluntary intake and animal performance are recommended when introducing legume forages into mixed diets</cite>. 
- Agronomy and varieties: Select drought‑tolerant, high‑fodder cultivars for pigeon pea and Lablab; manage spacing, cutting height/interval to optimize dry matter yield and digestibility; for Stylosanthes and Desmodium, plan harvest timing and consider pit silos or bale silage to manage palatability and fermentation <cite id="49380809-2">Spacing and cutting interval affect pigeon pea fodder yield and nutritional value; palatability and tolerance to grazing/cutting are key selection criteria</cite><cite id="8982ac66-0">Seasonal production and palatability issues require storage and management to maintain feed value</cite>. 
- Research agenda: Expand multi‑disciplinary trials on underutilized legumes integrating agronomy, processing, and animal science; develop standardized inclusion guidelines by species and form (fresh, hay, silage, pelleted) with attention to anti‑nutrient mitigation; breed for feed traits (higher CP, lower fiber, better digestibility, lower trypsin inhibitor/lectin content); build extension capacity and farmer‑participatory trials for adoption at scale <cite id="6fe0d352-3">Breeding and domestication of underutilized legumes for food/feed requires significant research and development to transform landraces into broadly adaptable, economically viable crops</cite><cite id="6fe0d352-0">Microbial inocula and natural tenderizers can be developed to improve growth, yield, and processing of underutilized legumes</cite>.

Summary
Underutilized leguminous crops such as cowpea, pigeon pea, Lablab, Stylosanthes, and others provide high‑quality protein and fiber for ruminants, with documented gains in intake, digestibility, and growth when properly managed and processed; their shrub/forage forms can be conserved as silages to overcome seasonality and palatability, and they can substitute for expensive protein sources in cattle diets while improving nitrogen cycling on farms <cite id="c96510d6-0">Cowpea forage and silage improve intake, growth, and digestibility for ruminants and provide nutritional benefits due to phenolics and tannins</cite><cite id="6fe0d352-2">Leguminous forages are affordable, improve production and reproduction, and supply nutrients in areas without agro‑industrial by‑products</cite><cite id="8982ac66-4">Stylosanthes silage can replace corn silage in feedlot beef cattle diets without affecting intake or performance</cite>. Effective adoption hinges on processing (ensiling, dehulling, heat treatment), cultivar selection, and extension support to mitigate anti‑nutritional factors and palatability issues; expanding breeding and agronomic research on underutilized legumes will further unlock their potential as sustainable, climate‑resilient feed resources for smallholder and commercial systems alike <cite id="6fe0d352-3">Underutilized legumes remain largely unexploited for feed; targeted breeding and research are required to enhance their adaptability and economic viability</cite><cite id="49380809-2">Pigeon pea’s multi‑purpose nature and drought tolerance make it a strong candidate for integrated crop‑livestock systems, pending improved management and extension</cite>.

Title: Potentials of underutilized legumes in food security
Snippet: A lot of microorganisms are associated with the nodules, rhizosphere, rhizoplane, and bulk soil of legumes generally, with few studies reporting these in underutilized legumes. Since underutilized legumes have the potentials to host novel microbes with desirable characteristics and traits to improve crop yield (such as the ability to survive in extreme temperature, pH, salinity and water stressed situation, their insecticidal and pesticidal ability and the potential to fix high nitrogen), such microbes should be developed into products such as inoculum, biofertilizers, biochar, biopesticides, bioinsecticides, etc. to increase the growth and yield of both leguminous and nonleguminous plants. Plant extracts can also be produced using different parts of underutilized legumes such as the roots, stems, pods, leaves, etc., and tested for their ability to treat plant diseases and drive away pests and insects. 

Underutilized legumes should be incorporated into different planting system so as to determine the best planting system that suits them and fully unleash their potentials to improve food security. Furthermore, the compatibility of underutilized crops with other crops, the principles underlying the transfer of nitrogen from nitrogen-fixing underutilized legumes to companion crops and the yield outcome during intercropping should be well understood in order to maximize the advantages associated with their intercropping. 

In addition, research should be intensified on the application of legumes to adapt and mitigate climate change effects which include pests, erosion, drought, salinity and diseases; this will help to maximize land resources. Also, organic tenderizers such as unripe pawpaw and kiwi which are being used locally as tenderizers to soften beefs while cooking, should be tested for their ability to reduce the cooking time of underutilized legumes by softening them, as organic tenderizers are natural and not associated with harmful side effects compared to their chemical counterparts. 

Due to the high nutritional and medicinal properties of many underutilized legumes, essential nutrients can be extracted from them and made into nutritional supplements or tablets for the treatment and prevention of ailments.
</snippet>

Title: Underutilized legumes: nutrient status and advanced breeding approaches for qualitative and quantitative enhancement
Snippet: Underutilized/orphan legumes provide food and nutritional security to resource-poor rural populations during periods of drought and extreme hunger, thus, saving millions of lives. The Leguminaceae, which is the third largest flowering plant family, has approximately 650 genera and 20,000 species and are distributed globally. There are various protein-rich accessible and edible legumes, such as soybean, cowpea, and others; nevertheless, their consumption rate is far higher than production, owing to ever-increasing demand. The growing global urge to switch from an animal-based protein diet to a vegetarian-based protein diet has also accelerated their demand. In this context, underutilized legumes offer significant potential for food security, nutritional requirements, and agricultural development. Many of the known legumes like Mucuna spp., Canavalia spp., Sesbania spp., Phaseolus spp., and others are reported to contain comparable amounts of protein, essential amino acids, polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), dietary fiber, essential minerals and vitamins along with other bioactive compounds. Keeping this in mind, the current review focuses on the potential of discovering underutilized legumes as a source of food, feed and pharmaceutically valuable chemicals, in order to provide baseline data for addressing malnutrition-related problems and sustaining pulse needs across the globe. There is a scarcity of information about underutilized legumes and is restricted to specific geographical zones with local or traditional significance. Around 700 genera and 20,000 species remain for domestication, improvement, and mainstreaming. Significant efforts in research, breeding, and development are required to transform existing local landraces of carefully selected, promising crops into types with broad adaptability and economic viability. Different breeding efforts and the use of biotechnological methods such as micro-propagation, molecular markers research and genetic transformation for the development of underutilized crops are offered to popularize lesser-known legume crops and help farmers diversify their agricultural systems and boost their profitability.
</snippet>

Title: Modulation of Bovine Wnt Signaling Pathway Genes by Cowpea Phenolic Extract
Snippet: Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata L.Walp) is an important annual legume plant used for food. It is cultivated and consumed largely in Africa, Asia, and South America. Cowpea seed grains are rich in protein: 27% (Gupta et al., 2010). Cowpea with a comparable yield and digestibility to alfafa (Cook, 2005), has high nutritive value, a crude protein of 22%, and are fed to animals as forage, hay or silage (Etana et al., 2013). Using cowpea as protein supplement feed has been recommended for ruminants fed low-quality roughages for improved productivity (Etana et al., 2013;Gwanzura et al., 2012). Cowpea was used as one of the summer legumes for cow and calves on Bermudagrass creep grazing pastures (Pitman et al., 2015). Supplementing small ruminant feed with cowpea forage enhanced feed intake, increased average daily gain, nitrogen intake and digestibility and fecal nitrogen output (Baloyi et al., 2008;Koralagama et al., 2008). Use of cowpea as summer finishing forage in cattle resulted in greater marbling score and increased dressing percentage and consumer steak preference (Schmidt et al., 2013). 

Cowpea contains phenolic compounds including phenol acids, flavonoids, and tannins (Cai et al., 2003). Due to their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticarcinogenic effects, these bioactive compounds pose an added health benefit to humans and animals (Lee & Yen, 2006;Balsano & Alisi, 2009;Folmer et al., 2014;Ojwang et al., 2015). In animal studies, flavonoids (Middleton et al., 2000) and condensed tannins (Min et al., 2004) have been reported to have benefits for ruminant health and productivity.

Title: Pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) fodder cutting management in the Guinea Savanna Agro-Ecological Zone of Ghana
Snippet: Pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan), is a perennial leguminous crop with several uses: grain, vegetable, animal feed, green manure, and firewood (Gowda et al. 2012). It is one of the best drought-resistant legumes (Bidlack et al. 2006) and is often the only grain plant that provides some grain yield for the period of dry spells when other legumes such as field beans have wilted and possibly dried up (Sharma et al. 2011). The plant has an erect growth pattern, it is a short-lived perennial leguminous shrub with a height of about 1-2 m, but can reach up to 2-5 m high (Bekele-Tessema 2007). 

Fodder from Cajanus cajan has been reported to increase the intake of low-quality fodder and enhances ruminant live weight due to its relatively higher nitrogen concentration (Shenkute et al. 2013). Pigeon pea fodder may be used in ruminant diets as a protein supplement even at higher levels of inclusion without any detrimental effect. The fodder is highly digestible and supply high quality protein when fed to ruminants (Corriher et al. 2007). Sheep and goats in Ghana, have been found to select leaves of Pigeon pea in preference to other legumes (Karbo et al. 1998). 

The cultivation of Pigeon pea as fodder, despite its forage potential, is not a common practice amongst smallholder farmers in Ghana. Pigeon pea is rather cultivated either as a border crop or on marginal lands for grains, fodder and fuel wood (Marfo 1990). At maturity, the pods are harvested and threshed to separate the grain from the husk. The husk, combined with dry leaves of the Pigeon pea are fed to ruminants (Agyare et al. 2002) by smallholder farmers practicing the crop/livestock production system. This makes Pigeon pea a very useful crop in the crop/livestock production system in Ghana. 

Tolerance to grazing or cutting is a very important consideration in selecting a plant for fodder production.
</snippet>

Some of these novel sources may have promising and desirable nutritive quality for future inclusion in animal diet. Legumes are important sources of protein and energy for farm animals. One of the under-utilize legumes of interest is the pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan). Pigeon pea is a useful feed source. Despite the large number of existing legume grains in Nigeria, only soybean, cotton seed cake and groundnut cake are mainly used in livestock feeding. Verdcourt), lima beans (Phaseolus lunatus L.), locust bean (Parkia species), African yam beans (Sphenostylis stenocarpa Hochst.), sunflower seed (Helianthus annuus L.), and pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan (L.) Millsp.) have been under-utilized and under-exploited for livestock feeding particularly in Nigeria (Apata & Ologhobo, 1994). There is the tendency to underestimate the significance of the novel legumes that are under-exploited; this category of legumes is often classified as minor legumes, resulting from inadequate information on their nutritional qualities, uses, and cultivations. Snippet: Cajanus cajan (pigeon pea) is a perennial member of family Fabaceae and is one of the most common legumes of the tropics and sub-tropics with a wide adaptability to poor soil conditions than most tropical legumes and drought tolerant (Akinola and Oyejola, 1994;Speranza et al., 2007, Crop Trust, 2014). Cajanus cajan is a glandular-pubescent, shortlived perennial (1-5 years) shrub, usually grown as an annual plant, 0.5-4 m high, with roots up to 15 -20cm deep; stems up to 15 cm in diameter; branches are many and slender. It is emerging as common domestic forage plants as they are raised in traditional home gardens in many parts of Nigeria. Pigeon peas are evergreen and could be used as a potential source of forage for ruminant animals year round. Pigeon pea is a multi-purpose nitrogen fixing plant that provides food, fuel wood, fodder and shelter material to subsistence farmers. The seeds can be used as animal feed and post-harvest products such as haulms, leaf and young stems have good fodder value. Pigeon pea has a prolonged cooking time and low food value for human when compared to cowpea (Amaefule and Obioha, 2001). Amaefule and Onwudike (2000) reported that pigeon pea is rich in nitrogen (21-30% CP), thus qualifies it as a suitable protein source of ruminant animal feed. These attributes have elicited interest among Animal Nutritionist on the need to explore and exploit further use of the plant/crop as an alternative source of plant protein for ruminants (Ahamefule et al., 2006). Seeds are sown where desired, in pure stands at about 9-22 kg/ha for rows, but sometimes it is broadcast. Seed germinates in about 2 weeks. Quite frequently (in India) pigeon pea is grown mixed with other crops are grown in alternate rows with rows of sorghum, groundnuts, sesame, cotton, pineapples, millets or maize.

Title: Effects of Different Moisture Levels and Additives on the Ensiling Characteristics and In Vitro Digestibility of Stylosanthes Silage
Snippet: The shortage of high-quality forage grass and protein feed is an important factor restricting the development of animal husbandry. Alfalfa, a high-quality protein forage resource, has been planted and utilized on a large scale worldwide [1]. Stylosanthes guianensis, a common flowering legume that is native to South America, grows mainly in tropical and subtropical regions. In the subtropics, it is considered an important feed source for ruminants, with high yields, high nutrient levels, and wide adaptability [2]. However, the surface of the Stylosanthes stalk is rough and hairy, and its palatability is poor. In addition, Stylosanthes is produced seasonally. If it cannot be harvested and used in time during its peak growth period in the summer, Stylosanthes will continue to grow until it ages, and its feed value will decrease, resulting in an insufficient supply of livestock feed in the winter and spring seasons [3]; therefore, storing it as silage would be highly beneficial. Silage quality is affected by many factors, and legumes such as Stylosanthes are difficult to ensile directly without additives because of their high buffering capacity, low water-soluble carbohydrate content, and high dry matter content [4]. 

During the silage process, the lactic acid bacteria attached to the surface of raw materials are fermented under anaerobic conditions to convert water-soluble carbohydrates (WSCs) into organic acids, mainly lactic acid. This rapidly acidifies the silage environment and inhibits the growth of harmful microorganisms; thus, the feed can be preserved for a long time [5]. Stylosanthes has characteristics such as a high buffering energy, low sugar content, and high moisture content at harvest, which are similar to those of alfalfa; hence, it is more difficult to prepare silage directly [6,7]. The use of additives is important for preparing high-quality silage.
</snippet>

Title: Effects of maize, ryegrass and sorghum silages on performance, meat quality and some blood variables of lambs
Snippet: The study was conducted at a private farm located in Sakarya province, Türkiye, at 40.8771° N latitude and 30.3790° E longitude. A total of 24 male Ile de France lambs were used and randomly allocated into four groups: control, maize silage, sorghum silage, and ryegrass silage. Prior to the feeding trial, lambs underwent a 14-day adaptation period during which all animals received the same basal concentrate diet, while the silage corresponding to their assigned treatment group was offered ad libitum. This standard adaptation protocol is widely used in small ruminant feeding studies to stabilize rumen function and minimize pre-experimental variation. 

During the experimental phase, the lambs were housed individually in pens measuring 1.5 × 1.5 meters and were provided with ad libitum access to their respective test diets and fresh water. Ad libitum feeding was ensured using a standard offer-refusal approach: silage or straw was offered twice daily (morning and evening) after being weighed; additional feed was supplied whenever an animal finished Spanish Journal of Agricultural Research, 24 (1), 2026, 21825 the provided amount, and refusals were collected and weighed before each feeding to determine actual intake. A refusal level of approximately 10% of the offered feed was maintained to guarantee continuous ad libitum availability. 

At the beginning of the trial, the average initial body weight of the lambs was 26.53±0.21 kg. The amount of concentrate feed was set at 2% of live body weight and adjusted biweekly based on weight gain (Table 2). The intake of the basal ration was not measured separately because alfalfa and sunflower meal were supplied in fixed daily amounts that did not vary across the experimental period. Only the lamb grower feed component was adjusted according to body weight, whereas daily silage or straw intake was recorded individually. The basal ration consisted of a fixed daily formulation of 0.075 kg alfalfa, 0.40 kg lamb grower feed, and 0.12 kg sunflower meal (Table 3).

Campo Grande silage fermented to pH ~4 with 5% lactic acid and ~3.6% acetic acid can replace corn silage in feedlot diets without affecting intake or performance</cite>.

Underutilized leguminous crops such as cowpea, pigeon pea, Lablab, Stylosanthes, and others provide high‑quality protein and fiber for ruminants, with documented gains in intake, digestibility, and growth when properly managed and processed; their shrub/forage forms can be conserved as silages to overcome seasonality and palatability, and they can substitute for expensive protein sources in cattle diets while improving nitrogen cycling on farms <cite id="c96510d6-0">Cowpea forage and silage improve intake, growth, and digestibility for ruminants and provide nutritional benefits due to phenolics and tannins</cite><cite id="6fe0d352-2">Leguminous forages are affordable, improve production and reproduction, and supply nutrients in areas without agro‑industrial by‑products</cite><cite id="8982ac66-4">Stylosanthes silage can replace corn silage in feedlot beef cattle diets without affecting intake or performance</cite>. Snippet: A lot of microorganisms are associated with the nodules, rhizosphere, rhizoplane, and bulk soil of legumes generally, with few studies reporting these in underutilized legumes. Since underutilized legumes have the potentials to host novel microbes with desirable characteristics and traits to improve crop yield (such as the ability to survive in extreme temperature, pH, salinity and water stressed situation, their insecticidal and pesticidal ability and the potential to fix high nitrogen), such microbes should be developed into products such as inoculum, biofertilizers, biochar, biopesticides, bioinsecticides, etc. to increase the growth and yield of both leguminous and nonleguminous plants. Underutilized legumes should be incorporated into different planting system so as to determine the best planting system that suits them and fully unleash their potentials to improve food security. Title: Modulation of Bovine Wnt Signaling Pathway Genes by Cowpea Phenolic Extract
Snippet: Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata L.Walp) is an important annual legume plant used for food. It is cultivated and consumed largely in Africa, Asia, and South America. Cowpea seed grains are rich in protein: 27% (Gupta et al., 2010). Cowpea with a comparable yield and digestibility to alfafa (Cook, 2005), has high nutritive value, a crude protein of 22%, and are fed to animals as forage, hay or silage (Etana et al., 2013). Using cowpea as protein supplement feed has been recommended for ruminants fed low-quality roughages for improved productivity (Etana et al., 2013;Gwanzura et al., 2012). Cowpea was used as one of the summer legumes for cow and calves on Bermudagrass creep grazing pastures (Pitman et al., 2015). Supplementing small ruminant feed with cowpea forage enhanced feed intake, increased average daily gain, nitrogen intake and digestibility and fecal nitrogen output (Baloyi et al., 2008;Koralagama et al., 2008). Use of cowpea as summer finishing forage in cattle resulted in greater marbling score and increased dressing percentage and consumer steak preference (Schmidt et al., 2013). 

Cowpea contains phenolic compounds including phenol acids, flavonoids, and tannins (Cai et al., 2003). Due to their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticarcinogenic effects, these bioactive compounds pose an added health benefit to humans and animals (Lee & Yen, 2006;Balsano & Alisi, 2009;Folmer et al., 2014;Ojwang et al., 2015). In animal studies, flavonoids (Middleton et al., 2000) and condensed tannins (Min et al., 2004) have been reported to have benefits for ruminant health and productivity.

Title: ENSILING QUALITY OF PEARL MILLET FORTIFIED WITH GRADED LEVELS OF COWPEA FORAGE
Snippet: The experiment was conducted to investigate the effect of cowpea (Vigna unguiculata L. Walp) forage inclusion on the ensiling quality of Pearl millet (Pennisetum typhoides Burm.F). Pearl millet and cowpea forages were mixed at 100:00, 80:20, 60:40, and 40:60, respectively and ensiled for 3 weeks in the laboratory silos. After fermentation period, the silos were opened and contents scored for colour, aroma and pH. Proximate composition and fiber analysis was carried, dry matter intake, dry matter digestibility, metabolizable energy and reference feed value was also estimated. The result revealed that the silages were moderately acidic, very sweet and had yellowish colour. Cowpea forage inclusion for ensiling pearl millet improved the CP, ash, EE, ME, dry matter digestibility, dry matter intake and RFV with corresponding declined in DM and fiber fractions. Cowpea forage inclusion at 60% level is recommended for ensiling pearl millet grass. Further studies to determine voluntary feed intake and animal performance are recommended.

Snippet: Pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan), is a perennial leguminous crop with several uses: grain, vegetable, animal feed, green manure, and firewood (Gowda et al. 2012). It is one of the best drought-resistant legumes (Bidlack et al. 2006) and is often the only grain plant that provides some grain yield for the period of dry spells when other legumes such as field beans have wilted and possibly dried up (Sharma et al. 2011). The plant has an erect growth pattern, it is a short-lived perennial leguminous shrub with a height of about 1-2 m, but can reach up to 2-5 m high (Bekele-Tessema 2007). 

Fodder from Cajanus cajan has been reported to increase the intake of low-quality fodder and enhances ruminant live weight due to its relatively higher nitrogen concentration (Shenkute et al. 2013). Pigeon pea fodder may be used in ruminant diets as a protein supplement even at higher levels of inclusion without any detrimental effect. The fodder is highly digestible and supply high quality protein when fed to ruminants (Corriher et al. 2007). Sheep and goats in Ghana, have been found to select leaves of Pigeon pea in preference to other legumes (Karbo et al. 1998). 

The cultivation of Pigeon pea as fodder, despite its forage potential, is not a common practice amongst smallholder farmers in Ghana. Pigeon pea is rather cultivated either as a border crop or on marginal lands for grains, fodder and fuel wood (Marfo 1990). At maturity, the pods are harvested and threshed to separate the grain from the husk. The husk, combined with dry leaves of the Pigeon pea are fed to ruminants (Agyare et al. 2002) by smallholder farmers practicing the crop/livestock production system. This makes Pigeon pea a very useful crop in the crop/livestock production system in Ghana. 

Tolerance to grazing or cutting is a very important consideration in selecting a plant for fodder production.

Title: Effects of Different Moisture Levels and Additives on the Ensiling Characteristics and In Vitro Digestibility of Stylosanthes Silage
Snippet: The shortage of high-quality forage grass and protein feed is an important factor restricting the development of animal husbandry. Alfalfa, a high-quality protein forage resource, has been planted and utilized on a large scale worldwide [1]. Stylosanthes guianensis, a common flowering legume that is native to South America, grows mainly in tropical and subtropical regions. In the subtropics, it is considered an important feed source for ruminants, with high yields, high nutrient levels, and wide adaptability [2]. However, the surface of the Stylosanthes stalk is rough and hairy, and its palatability is poor. In addition, Stylosanthes is produced seasonally. If it cannot be harvested and used in time during its peak growth period in the summer, Stylosanthes will continue to grow until it ages, and its feed value will decrease, resulting in an insufficient supply of livestock feed in the winter and spring seasons [3]; therefore, storing it as silage would be highly beneficial. Silage quality is affected by many factors, and legumes such as Stylosanthes are difficult to ensile directly without additives because of their high buffering capacity, low water-soluble carbohydrate content, and high dry matter content [4].

Overview
Many protein-rich leguminous plants have demonstrated nutritional adequacy for livestock but remain underutilized globally as feed due to constraints including feed shortages, rising costs of conventional feeds, anti-nutritional factors, and limited processing infrastructure in smallholder systems. <cite id="133334f6-0">Underutilized or orphan legumes span hundreds of genera and offer substantial potential for feed and food, yet research and domestication efforts lag, leaving many species underexploited despite comparable protein, amino acids, and minerals to major pulses</cite>. <cite id="133334f6-4">Grain legumes (chickpea, lentil, cowpea, pea, faba bean, lupin, bambara groundnut, velvet bean) provide plant-based protein for direct grazing or processed meals and are dual-purpose in crop–livestock systems, yet their fodder use remains underutilized and poorly documented in semi-arid tropics</cite>. <cite id="5c72c466-1">In tropical regions, bridging year‑round feed gaps requires expanding use of alternative nonconventional feed resources such as shrub legumes and tannin-rich plants, but evidence is fragmented and adoption is limited by quality and logistics</cite>.

What is underutilized and why
Evidence converges that underutilization reflects both supply-side scarcity and demand-side barriers. <cite id="5c72c466-1">Ruminant production is constrained by poor-quality roughages and feed shortages, with documented gaps (e.g., 3.5 million tons in Egypt) that motivate use of alternative feed resources</cite>. <cite id="5c72c466-4">Nonconventional feeds are pursued because conventional resources compete with human food and between monogastrics and ruminants; forage legumes supply high-quality protein and fermentable fiber but require processing and feeding strategies to realize their value</cite>. <cite id="133334f6-0">Despite adequate protein and micronutrients, many underutilized legumes lack domestication and development, leaving farmers and feed producers with limited adapted, viable seed and processing options</cite>.

Key underutilized leguminous crops for ruminant feeding
- Tropical pasture legumes: Sesbania spp., Desmodium spp., Indigofera spp.
  - Demonstrated nutritional adequacy and feed efficiency: <cite id="6e65d3f6-0">In sacco and in vitro studies rank Sesbania and Indigofera among the most rapidly degradable legumes for rumen DM, with the highest A+B degradability and effective degradation of dry matter digestibility (ED-DMD), outperforming acacia and other trees</cite>. <cite id="6e65d3f6-1">Sesbania leaves and whole forage show higher rumen degradability (A+B) and in vitro OM digestibility; Desmodium leaves have lower fiber and higher CP than twigs, and both species can supplement low-quality roughages to improve ruminant nutrition</cite>.
  - Constraints and underuse: <cite id="6e65d3f6-2">Indigofera species can contain indospicine, a toxic nonprotein amino acid that is hepatotoxic in ruminants; species selection (e.g., I. zollingeriana with low indospicine) is critical to avoid poisoning and ensure safe adoption</cite>. <cite id="6e65d3f6-3">Pellets from Indigofera zollingeriana mixed with cereal by-products often do not meet ruminant protein specifications, reflecting formulation and blending challenges in low-input systems</cite>.
  - Evidence of underutilization: <cite id="6e65d3f6-4">Field trials in Ethiopia show Sesbania leaves are promoted to supplement urea‑treated rice straw for small ruminants during feed scarcity, underscoring their role as an on‑farm, cheap protein source that remains comparatively underused versus commercial concentrates</cite>.

- Shrub and multipurpose tree legumes used in Africa and beyond

Title: Nutrient intake, digestibility, growth performance and carcass characteristics of Farta sheep fed urea-treated rice straw supplemented with graded levels of dried Sesbania sesban leaves
Snippet: Livestock production is an important component of the farming systems in all parts of Ethiopia and plays a vital role in the livelihood of many people. Sheep and goats are widely reared in a crop-livestock farming systems and are distributed across different agroecological zones of Ethiopia. They require smaller investments, have shorter production cycles and greater environmental adaptability and hence have a unique niche in smallholder agriculture. Although diverse sheep and goat resources are found in Ethiopia, their productivity is low mainly because of inadequate year-round nutrition, in terms of both quantity and quality [1]. Livestock in general and sheep in particular are getting their feed from natural pasture and crop residues. Among the crop residues, rice straw has become involved as livestock feed. Rice straw is abundantly available crop residues in most tropical and subtropical countries and commonly used as a diet for ruminants, although feeding only rice straw does not provide enough nutrients to the ruminants to maintain high production levels due to the low nutritive value of this highly lignified material. By treating rice straw with urea intake, degradability and growth can be enhanced, compared to feeding untreated rice straw alone [2]. 

Most investigations in animal nutrition have been conducted on supplementation of poor-quality roughages with concentrates [3]; however, concentrate feeds comprised of especially grains and oil seeds are expensive and highly valued as human food [4]. Moreover, agroindustrial by-products are inaccessible and unaffordable to smallholder farmers; hence, alternative supplementary feedstuffs produced on-farm other than commercial concentrates are very essential. In this regard, strategic supplementation of unexploited, cheap, less competitive and year-round available and easily accessible protein sources like Sesbania sesban could be a feasible alternative to mitigate protein deficiency in poor-quality feeds during periods of feed scarcity. Therefore, the current study was conducted to evaluate the effects of graded levels of Sesbania sesban leaves supplementation on feed intake, digestibility, live weight change and carcass characteristics of Farta sheep fed urea-treated rice straw as basal diet.

Overview
Many protein-rich leguminous plants have demonstrated nutritional adequacy for livestock but remain underutilized globally as feed due to constraints including feed shortages, rising costs of conventional feeds, anti-nutritional factors, and limited processing infrastructure in smallholder systems. <cite id="133334f6-0">Underutilized or orphan legumes span hundreds of genera and offer substantial potential for feed and food, yet research and domestication efforts lag, leaving many species underexploited despite comparable protein, amino acids, and minerals to major pulses</cite>. <cite id="133334f6-4">Grain legumes (chickpea, lentil, cowpea, pea, faba bean, lupin, bambara groundnut, velvet bean) provide plant-based protein for direct grazing or processed meals and are dual-purpose in crop–livestock systems, yet their fodder use remains underutilized and poorly documented in semi-arid tropics</cite>. <cite id="5c72c466-1">In tropical regions, bridging year‑round feed gaps requires expanding use of alternative nonconventional feed resources such as shrub legumes and tannin-rich plants, but evidence is fragmented and adoption is limited by quality and logistics</cite>.

What is underutilized and why
Evidence converges that underutilization reflects both supply-side scarcity and demand-side barriers. <cite id="5c72c466-1">Ruminant production is constrained by poor-quality roughages and feed shortages, with documented gaps (e.g., 3.5 million tons in Egypt) that motivate use of alternative feed resources</cite>. <cite id="5c72c466-4">Nonconventional feeds are pursued because conventional resources compete with human food and between monogastrics and ruminants; forage legumes supply high-quality protein and fermentable fiber but require processing and feeding strategies to realize their value</cite>. <cite id="133334f6-0">Despite adequate protein and micronutrients, many underutilized legumes lack domestication and development, leaving farmers and feed producers with limited adapted, viable seed and processing options</cite>.

Key underutilized leguminous crops for ruminant feeding
- Tropical pasture legumes: Sesbania spp., Desmodium spp., Indigofera spp.
  - Demonstrated nutritional adequacy and feed efficiency: <cite id="6e65d3f6-0">In sacco and in vitro studies rank Sesbania and Indigofera among the most rapidly degradable legumes for rumen DM, with the highest A+B degradability and effective degradation of dry matter digestibility (ED-DMD), outperforming acacia and other trees</cite>. <cite id="6e65d3f6-1">Sesbania leaves and whole forage show higher rumen degradability (A+B) and in vitro OM digestibility; Desmodium leaves have lower fiber and higher CP than twigs, and both species can supplement low-quality roughages to improve ruminant nutrition</cite>.

- Shrub and multipurpose tree legumes used in Africa and beyond
  - Fodder tree legumes (FTL) such as Leucaena, Gliricidia, Calliandra, and Acacia are noted for high CP, minerals, and degradability when used as supplements, but their adoption is uneven and often limited by palatability, toxicity (e.g., mimosine in Leucaena), and processing constraints; nonetheless, they function as strategic feed resources in dry seasons and crop–livestock systems. <cite id="5c72c466-3">FTL provide high-quality fodder at relatively low feeding costs, complement dry-season pastures, and improve nutrient utilization when integrated into smallholder systems</cite>. <cite id="6e65d3f6-0">Comparative degradability shows Gliricidia, Sesbania, and Indigofera achieve high ED‑DMD, reinforcing their potential; however, anti‑nutritional factors (e.g., condensed tannins in some species) can inhibit digestibility if not managed</cite>.

- Faba bean by-products and vetch
  - Demonstrated digestibility and historical feeding success: <cite id="133334f6-2">Digestibility studies show 30–47% w/w digestible alfalfa hay, 39–61% w/w faba bean pod, with early ruminant trials (1940) reporting roughly two‑thirds digestibility of pod meal; young pods have high digestibility due to lower lignification</cite>. <cite id="133334f6-3">Vetch (Vicia sativa) has been valued for livestock alongside other forage legumes, yet in many contexts its fodder potential in smallholders remains underexploited</cite>.

- Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) and pigeonpea (Vigna radiata/sesquipedalis)
  - Cowpea: widely grown as grain, but residues and leaves are commonly fed to ruminants; its use as a strategic supplement during feed scarcity is reported, yet formal adoption in ruminant ration balancing remains limited in many regions. <cite id="5c72c466-4">Groundnut haulms are fed to ruminants in West Africa, but utilization depends on processing, feeding strategies, and eating behavior; similar constraints apply to legume haulms and residues like cowpea</cite>.
  - Pigeonpea: pigeonpea grain and by-products are promising in monogastric feeds and as roughage; processing (e.g., extrusion) can unlock digestibility for poultry and swine. <cite id="5c72c466-0">Extrusion of pigeonpea (Cajanus cajan) and related grain legumes alters starch digestion kinetics and is highlighted to support expanded use in intensive monogastric feeds, indicating underexploited potential in processed feed forms</cite>.

Key underutilized leguminous crops for swine and poultry
- Crotalaria spp. (spurred leaves)
  - Demonstrated adequacy with constraints: <cite id="0921147d-0">Crotalaria mucronata and C. retusa show relatively low alkaloids and tannins, with measured tannins mainly in pods; digestibility tests support their potential, and low anti‑nutritional levels suggest usability as forage</cite>. <cite id="0921147d-0">Ruminants are generally more tolerant of anti‑nutrients than monogastrics, enabling use in ruminant feeds but raising caution for swine and poultry unless processed</cite>.
  - Underuse tempered by toxicity risk: <cite id="0921147d-1">In pigs, diets containing Crotalaria spectabilis seeds (0.2–0.6%) caused edema, pale mucous membranes, and liver lesions, with mortality observed, demonstrating toxicity at typical inclusion levels</cite>. <cite id="0921147d-4">Experimental broiler studies show Crotalaria seeds (e.g., C. lanceolata) are hepatotoxic; species vary in toxicity (e.g., C. pallida less than C. lanceolata), and clinical signs include inappetence, ascites, and yellowish liver lesions</cite>. These risks limit widespread monogastric adoption despite adequate protein content.

- Lupin (Lupinus spp.)
  - Monogastric potential with processing: lupin meal is nutritionally viable for swine and poultry when dehulled and thermally processed to reduce alkaloids; limited acceptance and supply-chain constraints persist, but evidence supports its use in balanced diets. <cite id="5c72c466-0">Processing innovations (e.g., extrusion) for grain legumes like Cajanus cajan are emphasized to improve digestibility and safety, illustrating a generalizable pathway for lupin meal via dehulling and heat treatment</cite>.

- Grain legumes beyond the major soybean/cowpea/pea: vetch, faba bean, lupin, bambara groundnut, velvet bean
  - These legumes supply plant‑based protein and fiber usable directly or blended with cereals; their adoption in monogastric feeds is underpinned by processing technologies (e.g., extrusion) that improve nutrient availability and safety. <cite id="133334f6-4">Legume residues and grains can be ground and used as animal feed; grain legumes have dual human–animal roles and are underused in fodder in smallholders’ systems</cite>. <cite id="5c72c466-0">Extrusion studies on legume grains highlight their nutritional implications for monogastrics and support expanded use as feed ingredients</cite>.

- Constraints to global utilization:
  - Anti‑nutritional factors and toxicity: <cite id="6e65d3f6-2">Indigofera’s indospicine can cause hepatotoxicity in ruminants, necessitating species selection and caution</cite>; <cite id="0921147d-1">Crotalaria toxicity in swine</cite>; <cite id="0921147d-4">broilers exposed to Crotalaria seeds show ascites and liver lesions</cite>.

  - Information gaps and domestication: <cite id="133334f6-0">Limited domestication and research leave many underutilized legumes in a state of local or regional knowledge with barriers to mainstreaming</cite>.

- Enablers:
  - Demonstrated nutrient adequacy and cost advantage: <cite id="133334f6-2">High digestibility of faba bean pods and historical ruminant success</cite>; <cite id="6e65d3f6-1">Sesbania and Desmodium provide sufficient macro/micro minerals and can supplement low‑quality roughages</cite>.
  - Systems integration: <cite id="5c72c466-3">Fodder tree legumes integrate into dry-season rotations and crop–livestock systems, offering low-cost, high‑quality feed that improves nutrient bioavailability</cite>. <cite id="133334f6-4">Legume residues fit smallholder systems and can be used directly or blended into complete meals</cite>.
  - Technology and policy: <cite id="5c72c466-0">Extrusion and processing research supports adoption of underused legumes in monogastric feeds</cite>; targeted screening and breeding can reduce anti‑nutrients and improve traits for feed conversion. <cite id="133334f6-0">Breeding and biotechnology pathways (micropropagation, markers, transformation) are proposed to popularize underutilized legumes for food and feed</cite>.

Practical list: leguminous crops under-utilized for animal feeding with demonstrated nutritional adequacy
- Tropical forages (underused outside research contexts):
  - Sesbania spp. (leaves, pods, twigs): high rumen degradability and IVOMD; suitable as supplement to low-quality roughages; manage tannins and vary species/age. <cite id="6e65d3f6-0">Sesbania shows rapid rumen degradation and high ED‑DMD</cite> <cite id="6e65d3f6-1">Sesbania leaves/whole forage have higher A+B and IVOMD</cite>.
  - Desmodium spp. (e.g., Greenleaf): high IVOMD and CP in leaves; good supplement; be aware of condensed tannins and regional adaptation. <cite id="6e65d3f6-1">Desmodium leaves lower NDF/ADF and high CP; suitable supplement</cite>.
  - Indigofera spp. (e.g., I. zollingeriana with low indospicine): high palatability and protein; safe selections can avoid hepatotoxicity and be used as ruminant feed; formulation quality often suboptimal. <cite id="6e65d3f6-0">High ED‑DMD in Indigofera</cite> <cite id="6e65d3f6-2">Choose low‑indospicine species to avoid poisoning</cite> <cite id="6e65d3f6-3">Pellets often do not meet protein specs without better blends</cite>.
  - Crotalaria spp. (e.g., C. mucronata, C. retusa): acceptable forage when anti‑nutrients are low; avoid monogastric feeding unless processed due to pyrrolizidine alkaloid risks. <cite id="0921147d-0">Low alkaloids/tannins in C. mucronata/retusa; ruminant tolerance higher than monogastrics</cite> <cite id="0921147d-1">Swine toxicity reported with C. spectabilis</cite> <cite id="0921147d-4">Broiler toxicity observed with C. lanceolata</cite>.
- Faba bean and related Fabaceae:
  - Faba bean pods and by‑products: substantial digestibility; historical success in ruminant feeding; underused outside specific value chains. <cite id="133334f6-2">39–61% w/w digestible faba bean pods; ~75% digestibility of NFE; early pod-meal trials in sheep showed satisfactory digestibility</cite>.
  - Vetch (Vicia spp.): established forage legume with livestock value; underutilized as a major commercial feed ingredient outside Europe/regions. <cite id="133334f6-3">Vetch is part of forage legume set used in livestock production</cite>.
- Grain legumes with underused feed potential:
  - Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata): residues and grain used in many smallholder systems; underused in formal ruminant rations; toxicity concerns in some accessions. <cite id="5c72c466-4">Cowpea is a major legume in West Africa; haulms and residues are fed to ruminants when available</cite>.
  - Pigeonpea (Vigna radiata/sesquipedalis) and related Vigna: promising protein sources for ruminants and, when processed (e.g., extruded), for swine/poultry. <cite id="5c72c466-0">Extrusion improves digestibility kinetics and supports expanded monogastric use</cite>.
  - Lupin (Lupinus spp.): viable protein in swine/poultry feeds when dehulled and heat-treated; limited by alkaloids and supply chains. <cite id="5c72c466-0">Processing unlocks nutritional value for monogastrics</cite>.
  - Vetch, lupin, bambara groundnut, velvet bean: all provide plant-based protein; utilization is often localized and underdocumented globally. <cite id="133334f6-4">Legumes listed are fed directly or blended; dual-purpose in smallholder systems</cite>.

Evidence gaps and outlook
The literature consistently shows that underutilized legumes are nutritionally adequate for animal diets when properly managed, but adoption is limited by anti‑nutritional factors, processing know-how, and supply-chain issues. <cite id="133334f6-0">Scarcity of domestication and development hampers scaling</cite>, while feed shortages and rising costs in conventional inputs increase the incentive to deploy these alternatives. <cite id="5c72c466-1">Strategic use of shrub and multipurpose tree legumes can bridge gaps</cite>, and processing technologies like extrusion and dehulling can unlock monogastric feeds. <cite id="5c72c466-0">Research screening and processing innovations are key enablers</cite>. Title: Underutilized legumes: nutrient status and advanced breeding approaches for qualitative and quantitative enhancement
Snippet: Underutilized/orphan legumes provide food and nutritional security to resource-poor rural populations during periods of drought and extreme hunger, thus, saving millions of lives. The Leguminaceae, which is the third largest flowering plant family, has approximately 650 genera and 20,000 species and are distributed globally. There are various protein-rich accessible and edible legumes, such as soybean, cowpea, and others; nevertheless, their consumption rate is far higher than production, owing to ever-increasing demand. The growing global urge to switch from an animal-based protein diet to a vegetarian-based protein diet has also accelerated their demand. In this context, underutilized legumes offer significant potential for food security, nutritional requirements, and agricultural development. Many of the known legumes like Mucuna spp., Canavalia spp., Sesbania spp., Phaseolus spp., and others are reported to contain comparable amounts of protein, essential amino acids, polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), dietary fiber, essential minerals and vitamins along with other bioactive compounds. Keeping this in mind, the current review focuses on the potential of discovering underutilized legumes as a source of food, feed and pharmaceutically valuable chemicals, in order to provide baseline data for addressing malnutrition-related problems and sustaining pulse needs across the globe. There is a scarcity of information about underutilized legumes and is restricted to specific geographical zones with local or traditional significance. Around 700 genera and 20,000 species remain for domestication, improvement, and mainstreaming. Significant efforts in research, breeding, and development are required to transform existing local landraces of carefully selected, promising crops into types with broad adaptability and economic viability. Different breeding efforts and the use of biotechnological methods such as micro-propagation, molecular markers research and genetic transformation for the development of underutilized crops are offered to popularize lesser-known legume crops and help farmers diversify their agricultural systems and boost their profitability.

Title: Potentials of underutilized legumes in food security
Snippet: A lot of microorganisms are associated with the nodules, rhizosphere, rhizoplane, and bulk soil of legumes generally, with few studies reporting these in underutilized legumes. Since underutilized legumes have the potentials to host novel microbes with desirable characteristics and traits to improve crop yield (such as the ability to survive in extreme temperature, pH, salinity and water stressed situation, their insecticidal and pesticidal ability and the potential to fix high nitrogen), such microbes should be developed into products such as inoculum, biofertilizers, biochar, biopesticides, bioinsecticides, etc. to increase the growth and yield of both leguminous and nonleguminous plants. Plant extracts can also be produced using different parts of underutilized legumes such as the roots, stems, pods, leaves, etc., and tested for their ability to treat plant diseases and drive away pests and insects. 

Underutilized legumes should be incorporated into different planting system so as to determine the best planting system that suits them and fully unleash their potentials to improve food security. Furthermore, the compatibility of underutilized crops with other crops, the principles underlying the transfer of nitrogen from nitrogen-fixing underutilized legumes to companion crops and the yield outcome during intercropping should be well understood in order to maximize the advantages associated with their intercropping. 

In addition, research should be intensified on the application of legumes to adapt and mitigate climate change effects which include pests, erosion, drought, salinity and diseases; this will help to maximize land resources. Also, organic tenderizers such as unripe pawpaw and kiwi which are being used locally as tenderizers to soften beefs while cooking, should be tested for their ability to reduce the cooking time of underutilized legumes by softening them, as organic tenderizers are natural and not associated with harmful side effects compared to their chemical counterparts. 

Due to the high nutritional and medicinal properties of many underutilized legumes, essential nutrients can be extracted from them and made into nutritional supplements or tablets for the treatment and prevention of ailments.
